strengths: The authors cover a broad spectrum of models, including proprietary and open-weight LLMs.
They thoroughly explore feedback settings across multiple types—compilation, execution, and verbal.
Extensive ablation studies and analyses reveal findings that highlight key factors for advancing conversational coding tasks.
Evaluating LLMs in interactive environments is a significant and emerging area of study.
The diverse combination of different feedback is reasonable.
The introduction of static alternative ConvCodeBench reduces the overhead of real-time feedback generation making it scalable and practical for large-scale experiments.
The authors conduct comprehensive experiments covering 17 open- and closed-source LLMs.

As the authors have highlighted, evaluating multi-turn code generation is very difficult. By providing an environment with access to many diverse combinations of feedback, ConvCodeWorld could potentially be very useful to the research community, to hill-climb on multi-turn coding capabilities of LLMs.

The authors have been very thorough about exploring different types of scenarios, with partial/full execution feedback, and novice/expert-level verbal feedback. This allows more fine-grained evaluation.
There is an extensive analysis of performance of many different LLMs, and the key findings will likely be very interesting to the research community.

Feedback in code generation feels like a fairly understudied area. The premise of the paper is quite interesting in my opinion. The results are also neat, particularly how different models perform well under different feedback scenarios.

The fact that ConvCodeBench bootstraps existing code generation benchmarks is quite compelling. While the authors apply this towards BigCodeBench, it sounds like it would work for a wide variety of similar benchmarks.
The evaluation is quite comprehensive, and the experimental setup is easy to understand + sound.
Section 4.2.3 - Given the knowledge about how ReflectionCoder was trained, it is quite interesting to see that the model’s performance varies with the type of feedback provided.

The authors’ experiments reveal a number of interesting insights. I particularly liked how ConvCodeBench performance is shown to be a good proxy for ConvCodeWorld performance, and the relationship between MRR and recall.
weaknesses: While this paper offers valuable insights into evaluating conversational code generation, the topic itself is not new. Prior works like InterCode and MINT have explored compilation, execution, and verbal feedback mechanisms (see Table 6).

The paper’s clarity could be improved, particularly in the introduction. Expanding the background on conversational code generation tasks and typical settings would help readers appreciate the unique contributions of this work. Additionally, certain terminology, like "partial coverage" in Table 1, could be more explicitly explained.
Temperature settings for experiments are not specified. This detail is relevant as multi-turn interactions could benefit from more varied output.

The construction of the proposed dataset is insufficiently explained, particularly given the reported 29% success rate on BigCodeBench. This contrasts with single-turn performance on ConvCodeWorld, which appears higher.
Prompting methods lack clear definition. Both Section 4.1 and Appendix B are vague on this, with no explicit description of the prompt setup for experiments.
The construction of $f_v$ and $f_v^*$ is not well explained. Examples in Section 2.1.1 and Appendix F could be enhanced with a more formal, detailed breakdown of these prompt components.
In Section A.3, could the authors clarify the meaning of "a model referenced ground truth code in $f_v^*$"? Why would the model reference ground truth, and could examples illustrate this behavior?
The novelty of this paper appears limited because prior work (MINT) already includes multi-turn interaction with execution results and human feedback; more comparisons with MINT are needed.

The simulated expert-level verbal feedback shown in Figure 13 is overly detailed and well-structured, raising concerns that it may not accurately reflect real expert feedback; an analysis comparing simulated to actual human feedback is needed.

The simulated novice-level verbal feedback shown in Figure 12 includes unrealistic information for novice programmers, raising concerns about its authenticity; an analysis comparing simulated to actual human feedback is needed.
The process of using partial execution feedback was not clearly explained, including how test cases were randomly omitted and what criteria ensured reasonable selection.

The claim that weaker models with feedback surpass single-turn SOTA models is an unfair comparison because weaker models benefit from additional input context; a fair comparison should evaluate the same LLMs in both single-turn and multi-turn scenarios.
The use of pre-generated feedback logs from a reference model in ConvCodeBench seems biased, as errors made by the reference model may not reflect errors the target model would encounter.

The calculated correlation between ConvCodeWorld and ConvCodeBench based on MRR and Recall may be unreasonable due to the aforementioned bias; a better way would be to show correlation of error patterns between the reference and target models.

The static benchmark ConvCodeBench may not constitute a true multi-turn evaluation because the output from previous turn is pre-defined and does not reflect the model's iterative improvement, making the setting unnatural.
The environment is constrained to Python only.
Section 2.1.1 relies heavily on references to the appendix, requiring frequent back-and-forth, and could benefit from including essential information directly in the main paper.
The mathematical notation is formalized correctly but harms readability; readers would prefer straightforward description of feedback types rather than mapping symbols.
Takeaway 2 in Section 4.2.1 lacks a detailed explanation for observed trends, providing only a coarse-grained justification.
The takeaway that feedback helps weaker models perform stronger than stronger models in a zero-shot setting is not surprising given prior work (e.g., Mint, InterCode).
